title: Short Stuff: Mason-Dixon Line
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Mason-Dixon Line. Josh explains how he learned of Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon from a Jeopardy clue, then covers the 1760s boundary dispute between William Penn's Pennsylvania Colony and Lord Baltimore (Charles Calvert) of Maryland, the 1763-1767 survey of 233 miles that took fifty-eight months, the survey equipment (zenith sector, plumb lines, telescopes), the limestone milestones and crown stones, the modern recalculation and the Mason Dixon Line Preservation Partnership's inventory, and how the line later became the informal North-South divide after Maryland's slave status and the 1820 Missouri Compromise. Closes with a side note on Maryland's status and enslaved people escaping across the border into Pennsylvania.

segments.title: Jeopardy clue sparks interest in Mason and Dixon
segments.summary: Josh says a Jeopardy clue about surveyors Mason and Dixon prompted him to research them, and mentions the article he found.

segments.title: Penn and Calvert boundary dispute
segments.summary: The hosts describe the decades-long dispute between William Penn's Pennsylvania Colony and Lord Baltimore (Charles Calvert) of Maryland, including the Philadelphia mapping problem and the roughly 4,000 square miles at stake.

segments.title: Commissioning the 1763 survey
segments.summary: In 1763 the King of England commissioned Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon to survey the boundary; the survey took fifty-eight months and covered about 233 miles.

segments.title: Accuracy of the survey and modern recalculation
segments.summary: Modern surveyors using satellites have recalculated the line and found Mason and Dixon's work nearly exact.

segments.title: Expedition costs, party, and equipment
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the supply list (including whiskey, brandy and wine), the pay the surveyors received, the party of about 120 people with Iroquois guides, and the zenith sector and plumb line used to measure star angles.

segments.title: Milestones, crown stones and the first geodetic survey
segments.summary: The surveyors placed limestone milestones every mile and carved crown stones every five miles, shipped from England, with C and P carvings. The survey was the first geodetic survey in North America. Later, the Mason Dixon Line Preservation Partnership inventoried the markers, finding all but ten.

segments.title: Line becomes the North-South divide
segments.summary: The line was used to divide North and South after 1820, because Maryland was a slave state and the Missouri Compromise tied slave states to the South. The hosts note Maryland's and Virginia's Southern identities.

segments.title: Maryland, Pennsylvania border and escape to freedom
segments.summary: Hosts note that enslaved people who crossed from Maryland into Pennsylvania between 1820 and 1850 were free, and mention the Fugitive Slave Act.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and point listeners to the source article hosted on the Maryland Bar Association website.
